definitionBean.title: Matrix Operations, Symmetric & Skew-Symmetric Matrices (Quick Revision)
definitionBean.definition: An ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions is called a matrix. A matrix having m rows and n columns has order m × n.
definitionBean.explanation: Addition and multiplication of matrices are possible only when their respective orders are suitable. The transpose of a matrix A' (or Aᵀ) is obtained by interchanging rows and columns. If A' = A, it is symmetric, and if A' = -A, it is a skew-symmetric matrix.
importantPoints: Matrix Addition: Corresponding elements of matrices of the same order are added
Matrix Multiplication: Product AB (m×p) of A (m×n) and B (n×p) is possible (Columns of first = Rows of second)
In general, matrix multiplication is not commutative: AB ≠ BA
Properties of Transpose: (A')' = A, (A + B)' = A' + B', (AB)' = B'A' (Reversal Law)
Skew-symmetric Matrix: A' = -A (All elements on its main diagonal are zero)
Every square matrix can be expressed as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix: A = 1/2(A + A') + 1/2(A - A')

parts.explanation:
1. Symmetric Matrix: A square matrix A is called symmetric if the transpose of A is equal to A, i.e., A' = A (or aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ for all i, j).
2. Skew-symmetric Matrix: A square matrix A is called skew-symmetric if the transpose of A is equal to -A, i.e., A' = -A (or aᵢⱼ = -aⱼᵢ for all i, j). All elements of its main diagonal are zero (aᵢᵢ = 0).

parts.statement: Prove that all diagonal elements of a skew-symmetric matrix are zero.
parts.explanation:
Step 1: By definition of skew-symmetric matrix: aᵢⱼ = -aⱼᵢ.
Step 2: Putting i = j for main diagonal elements: aᵢᵢ = -aᵢᵢ.
Step 3: Transposing: aᵢᵢ + aᵢᵢ = 0 ⇒ 2aᵢᵢ = 0 ⇒ aᵢᵢ = 0.
Hence, it is proved that all diagonal elements of a skew-symmetric matrix are zero.

parts.statement: If A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]], find the value of 2A + 3B.
parts.explanation:
Step 1: Scalar multiplication 2A = 2 × [[1, 2], [3, 4]] = [[2, 4], [6, 8]].
Step 2: Scalar multiplication 3B = 3 × [[5, 6], [7, 8]] = [[15, 18], [21, 24]].
Step 3: Adding corresponding elements:
2A + 3B = [[2 + 15, 4 + 18], [6 + 21, 8 + 24]] = [[17, 22], [27, 32]].

Step 1: For subtracting matrices, corresponding elements are subtracted:
A - B = [[2 - 1, 4 - 3], [3 - (-2), 2 - 5]].
Step 2: Solving: = [[1, 1], [3 + 2, -3]] = [[1, 1], [5, -3]].

parts.statement: If A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[2, 0], [1, 3]], find the product AB.
Is matrix multiplication generally commutative? Give an explanation.
parts.explanation: No, in general matrix multiplication is not commutative, i.e., AB ≠ BA. Often if AB is defined, BA may not even be defined, or even if they are of the same order, the products come out to be different.

parts.statement: Prove that for any square matrix A, (A + A') is always a symmetric matrix.
parts.explanation:
Step 1: Let P = A + A'.
Step 2: Taking transpose of both sides: P' = (A + A')'.
Step 3: Applying properties (A + B)' = A' + B' and (A')' = A:
P' = A' + (A')' = A' + A.
Step 4: Matrix addition is commutative (A' + A = A + A'):
P' = A + A' = P.
Since P' = P, (A + A') is a symmetric matrix. Hence proved.

parts.statement: Prove that (A - A') is always a skew-symmetric matrix.
parts.explanation:
Step 1: Let Q = A - A'. Taking transpose: Q' = (A - A')' = A' - (A')' = A' - A.
Step 2: Taking negative sign common: Q' = -(A - A') = -Q.
Step 3: Since Q' = -Q, (A - A') is always a skew-symmetric matrix.

parts.statement: If A = [[cos α, sin α], [-sin α, cos α]], verify that A'A = I (Identity Matrix).
parts.explanation:
Step 1: A' = [[cos α, -sin α], [sin α, cos α]].
Step 2: Finding product A'A:
A'A = [[cos α, -sin α], [sin α, cos α]] [[cos α, sin α], [-sin α, cos α]]
= [[cos²α + (-sin α)(-sin α), cos α sin α + (-sin α) cos α], [sin α cos α + cos α(-sin α), sin²α + cos²α]]
Step 3: = [[cos²α + sin²α, cos α sin α - sin α cos α], [sin α cos α - sin α cos α, sin²α + cos²α]]
= [[1, 0], [0, 1]] = I. Hence proved.
A square matrix A is called an orthogonal matrix if the product of the matrix and its transpose is the identity matrix I, i.e., A · A' = A' · A = I (where A' = A⁻¹).
